I often hear historians say that the South was a feudalistic entity. It was to an extent, but essentially its very ways fit right in the framework of American democracy, as American democracy was not built on equal rights and access to privilege without there being some qualifications, such as possession of private property, to participate in the social and political aspects of the political system. People tend to forget that slaves, especially in Louisiana and Virginia, until of course Nat Turner's rebellion, were allowed to own guns(people would be shocked by this), were allowed to have a few farm animals, and were allowed to freely float about at the permission of their masters, sometimes into town, to buy certain goods they wished.

In the Deep South, things were not necessarily so nice, and it was truly more of a system of chattel slavery, but there was also a desire to manumit certain slaves that were considered of great capacity or deserving of their freedom. There were some large free-colored and multi-colored populations in the Carolinas, but that area of Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, and to a lesser extent, Florida, were genuinely into the whole phenomenon of ensuring slaves knew their place(even very white looking slaves, which sort of makes one question the whole system of slavery, since you had relatives owning relatives and this is somewhat of a sad phenomenon and there was something biblical/Middle-Eastern about it, which is not to be liked).

Of course, this occurred in order to reinforce notions of social and class status, and part of it shows how oppressive slavery was to an extent, in so far as it did not allow people to reach their full potential, but this is a flaw the North knew how to remedy and ensure never was the case in their society. Of course, people tend to forget that social formation and economic mobility and profits for the sake of the property owner are considered of greater emphasis than educational formation(this is something the North emphasized more than the South, even if Southern education was better than Northern). I certainly agree that there is something Spartan about the South, but I'd say the South was far more Athenian than the North and had an opener culture of dialogue and a greater emphasis on reason, while the North based their whole notions of society on practicality and ideo-religious conformity, which was not necessarily the case in the South. The Spartans were out in the West, keeping a socio-legal eye on the preservation of Western society, herding, branding, and leading on their livestock, fighting over petty land squabble/stealing cattle, and getting involved in feudal fights.

The South was more of an agriculturalist aristocracy with a strong element of direct democracy(localized democracy) and the North was essentially a Republican oligarchy built on a kind of social democracy/communalism, which is where we get the notion that the North was more egalitarian, when in fact I think the South strove to be much more egalitarian(aside from building their society on race(Northern society revolved around social status more so than not). I think the whole notion that Southern society was harsh and rigid is kind of a misconception that has to do with liberal notions of how society works and in fact the whole process of slavery required ensuring the slaves were bequeathed to certain farmers for a brief period of time to be branded and made ready to work as slaves for the plantation owner.

This is Virginia I am talking about, but supposedly there was a plantation owner in Virginia who had socials, with all the goods usually found at socials, and a service that was conducted beforehand for the slaves which was hosted by the plantation owner himself. This was certainly something that only happened on smaller plantations, while in the coastal regions or the Mississippi Delta region, slaves had much less freedoms and niceties and were subject to a rigid and regimented life of work and worship(at best perhaps there was some monastic quality to it, where slaves had very little interaction with the world, but were content, as Africans, with not interacting with what would have been a white and unfriendly world surrounding them).

I think its an exaggeration to say the South was a tyrannical oligarchic society(that is more what Abraham Lincoln represented and that was his perception of the South and it was a perception held by merchants and farmers in the Upland South/Ohio River area, in my opinion. The South was oligarchic though, while the North was much more atomized and communal with a rather collectivist/populist leadership that ruled as the people on behalf of the people(more in line with the original vision of the founding fathers). As it concerns the morality of systems like slavery, it is a system of evil, and even though Aquinas claims that it is an evil that is necessary and from which good can come(I agree with this to an extent), it mostly a system that inclines man's passions towards greed and tyranny and binds man in a state where he cannot reach his full potential and is subject not to the laws of nature or some common sensical notion of morality that can be applied back to nature, but to the laws of a particular foreign society and the laws of a particular people.

I find that this can be quite egregious and its a system that favors ignorance and naivety because it keeps people from revolting against such a system and realizing its inherent issues(but keeps it at a merely unconscious kind of level). I sort of have an issue, and it was necessary to keeping the Southern economy going, but blacks should have been given some rudimentary education and in special cases, if they showed skill in specific subject matters, given an education in that subject matter, since it might have enhanced their practical/technical and even there labor skills(as education did not afford social and class status as it does today and it only empowers oneself to such an extent within society).

Of course, African-Americans were allowed to congregate and have meetings, to have services, and to read stuff like the Bible, and to be honest some whites were really thought to be only good for this, so in the grand scheme of things the South was quite an idyllic place to be versus the industrialized and commercialized North, where money was a God, people were seen as herds, and children and women were enslaved to work in industrial plants. Slavery could even be considered a practical good, because it built up the economies of the new world and gave whites a capacity to live a life of leisure and high-thought(whatever sense this might mean to man's understanding of how this concept applies back to both society and reality).

The main problem is it can turn into a system of capitalistic and consumeristic glut, but the oligarchic aspect of the plantation system ensured this never became the case. I think in essence ideas and abstract forms, such as morality, trumps the importance of practicality to an extent(in a indeterministic constructivist sense), but I think the South was aware of this and was trying to move towards a more industrialized society, but did not know how to deal with the issue surrounding slavery, but to make a national phenomenon, so that when slavery reached the end of its trek there was a way to ensure socially and economically emancipation did not disrupt the entire system in the long-term.
